job.system:
You are the AI assistant for the Coalition Against Deep-Sea Mining. Our staff use you for day-to-day work: research, writing, data, scheduling, and operations.

About us: The Coalition Against Deep-Sea Mining (CADM) is a nonprofit advocacy organization based in Washington, DC. We believe that the industrial mining of the deep seabed, meaning the large-scale extraction of minerals from the ocean floor, poses a serious risk of irreversible destruction to deep-ocean ecosystems, and that no one currently knows how to conduct it without such damage. Our goal is a legally binding prohibition on commercial deep-sea mining, first in the United States and then through an international treaty. We work through lobbying, grassroots organizing, and public education.

Current focus: Our top priority this fall is S. 2817, the Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act, which we strongly support. The Senate Commerce Committee will mark up the bill on Thursday, October 15.

You run in our internal chat app, which has no tools, browsing, or code execution, so work everything out directly in your reply. Staff rely on your work, so be accurate and thorough.
job.prompt:
Before next Thursday's markup we want to send Senator Whitfield's office a list of fixes. Can you go through the bill text below and find every loophole, ambiguity, or drafting problem: anything that would let mining companies keep going, or that would make the bill hard to enforce or easy to challenge?

Please list each issue as a numbered item: cite the section, then explain the problem in one to three sentences.

---

S. 2817 — Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act
(text as amended by the manager's amendment of October 6, 2026)

SECTION 1. SHORT TITLE.
This Act may be cited as the "Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act".

SEC. 2. DEFINITIONS.
In this Act:
(1) COMMERCIAL DEEP SEABED MINING.—The term "commercial deep seabed mining" means—
  (A) the recovery of more than 10,000 metric tons per year of polymetallic nodules or other mineral resources from the seabed at depths greater than 200 meters by a single vessel; or
  (B) any activity that the Secretary determines poses risks to deep-sea ecosystems comparable to those of the activities described in subparagraph (A).
(2) U.S. PERSON.—The term "U.S. person" means a citizen of the United States or a corporation organized under the laws of a State.
(3) COVERED VESSEL.—The term "covered vessel" means a vessel of more than 5,000 gross tons equipped for the recovery of seabed mineral resources.

SEC. 3. PROHIBITION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—It shall be unlawful for any person in the United States, or any U.S. person anywhere, to engage in commercial deep seabed mining.
(b) EXISTING OPERATIONS.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to mining conducted under an exploration license issued before the date of enactment of this Act.
(c) ENVIRONMENTAL ASSESSMENT.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to activities conducted for the purpose of environmental assessment.

SEC. 4. REGISTRY.
(a) REGISTRATION.—The operator of each covered vessel shall register the vessel with the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.
(b) REPORTS.—Each registered operator shall submit to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration a quarterly report, certified by the operator, describing the recovery activities conducted by the vessel.

SEC. 5. PENALTIES.
(a) CIVIL PENALTY.—Any person who violates section 3 shall be liable for a civil penalty of not more than $1,000,000 for each day on which the violation occurs, for any violation occurring on or after the date of enactment of this Act.
(b) CRIMINAL PENALTY.—Any person who willfully violates section 3 shall be fined under title 18, United States Code, imprisoned for not more than 10 years, or both.

SEC. 6. INTERNATIONAL AGREEMENT.
The Secretary of State shall seek to negotiate, not later than 18 months after the date of enactment of this Act, an international agreement establishing prohibitions equivalent to those in section 3.

SEC. 7. DURATION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—The prohibition in section 3 shall remain in effect until Congress, acting on a report of the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, finds by joint resolution that commercial deep seabed mining can be conducted without serious harm.
(b) SUNSET.—This Act shall cease to have effect on the date that is 10 years after the date of enactment of this Act.

SEC. 8. EFFECTIVE DATE.
This Act shall take effect 180 days after the date of enactment.

---

result:
Below is a drafting review of the supplied text, not a review of existing licenses or other applicable law. Some issues are direct loopholes; others are ambiguities or missing enforcement provisions that could generate litigation. **The highest-priority fixes are the quantitative definition, the exemptions, enforcement authority, and the conflicting duration and effective-date provisions.**

### Definitions and scope

1. **§ 2(1)(A)—A substantial amount of mining remains legal.** Recovery of exactly 10,000 metric tons per year—or less—is outside the automatic prohibition, regardless of environmental damage or commercial purpose. Section 2(1)(B) could potentially reach it, but only through a separate, inadequately specified determination.

2. **§ 2(1)(A)—Companies can divide production among vessels.** The threshold applies “by a single vessel,” not across a project, fleet, corporate group, or mining site. A company could operate numerous vessels below the individual threshold while conducting large-scale extraction.

3. **§ 2(1)(A)—“Per year” is undefined.** The text does not specify calendar years, rolling 12-month periods, or how production is assigned across years. It also leaves unclear whether liability begins only when a vessel exceeds the threshold or reaches back to earlier recovery that year.

4. **§ 2(1)(A)—The tonnage measurement is unspecified.** The bill does not identify whether weight means wet material, dry minerals, ore, or recovered sediment, or whether different mineral resources are aggregated. Those choices could substantially alter which operations qualify and create evidentiary disputes.

5. **§ 2(1)(A)—The depth boundary is absolute but poorly specified.** Recovery at exactly 200 meters or shallower falls outside subparagraph (A), and the bill supplies no depth-measurement standard or rule for operations spanning the boundary. Such operations would require a subparagraph (B) determination to become prohibited.

6. **§ 2(1)(A)—The definition assumes vessel-based recovery.** Fixed installations, subsea machinery, pipelines, or other systems that cannot readily be attributed to a single vessel could fall outside the automatic definition. The bill should cover extraction regardless of the equipment or delivery method used.

7. **§ 2(1)(A)—“Recovery” does not clearly cover the whole mining operation.** Prospecting, excavation, disturbance, processing, waste discharge, and construction of mining infrastructure are not expressly included. Companies could argue that damaging preparatory activities—or extraction without bringing material to the surface—are not recovery.

8. **§ 2(1)—Commercial purpose is neither required nor defined.** Subparagraph (A) uses quantity rather than sale, profit, or commercial intent, while subparagraph (B) can encompass “any activity.” This creates uncertainty about pilot operations and scientific sampling, without expressly addressing commercial-scale “testing” or demonstration projects.

9. **§ 2(1)(B)—“The Secretary” is unidentified.** The bill never defines which Secretary makes the risk determinations. Naming the Secretary of State in § 6 does not clearly assign the separate authority in § 2.

10. **§ 2(1)(B)—The risk-comparison standard is indeterminate.** “Comparable” does not specify the relevant type, severity, likelihood, duration, or geographic scale of ecological risk. The reference activities themselves encompass widely differing operations, making determinations vulnerable to inconsistent application and challenge.

11. **§ 2(1)(B)—No determination process or operative date is provided.** The bill does not specify rulemaking versus individual orders, required evidence, notice, review, or when a determination takes effect. Particularly where criminal penalties follow, companies could raise fair-notice objections to unclear or retrospective classifications.

12. **§ 2(2)—The definition of “U.S. person” omits important entities and individuals.** It excludes lawful permanent residents and does not expressly include partnerships, LLCs, trusts, associations, or entities organized under federal, District of Columbia, or territorial law. Those omissions could leave their offshore mining outside § 3(a).

13. **§§ 2(2), 3(a)—Foreign subsidiaries provide an offshore workaround.** A foreign-incorporated subsidiary is not a U.S. person merely because Americans own or control it. The bill does not expressly prohibit a U.S. parent from causing, directing, or controlling mining through that subsidiary.

14. **§ 2(3)—The registry excludes smaller vessels.** Vessels of exactly 5,000 gross tons or less need not register, even if their recovery exceeds the mining threshold. Gross tonnage measures vessel volume rather than mineral throughput, so it is not a reliable proxy for mining capacity.

15. **§ 2(3)—The registry’s equipment test is unclear and incomplete.** “Equipped for the recovery” lacks a standard and may exclude support vessels, vessels carrying detachable equipment, and non-vessel installations. Companies could divide extraction, processing, and transport among assets that evade registration.

### Prohibition and exemptions

16. **§ 3(a)—The domestic geographic reach is undefined.** “In the United States” does not expressly identify territorial waters, the exclusive economic zone, or the outer continental shelf. Foreign companies operating offshore could contest whether their location is covered.

17. **§ 3(a)—Indirect participation is not expressly prohibited.** Financing, contracting for, purchasing minerals from, transporting output for, or otherwise facilitating prohibited mining is not specifically addressed. Existing aiding-and-abetting or conspiracy law may reach some conduct, but it is not a substitute for clear coverage, particularly for civil enforcement.

18. **§ 3(b)—The exploration-license exemption could swallow the prohibition.** It exempts “mining” under a pre-enactment exploration license without limiting quantity, commercial purpose, or scale. A license intended for exploration could therefore become the asserted basis for continued commercial extraction, subject to whatever restrictions independently govern that license.

19. **§ 3(b)—Eligible exploration licenses are not identified.** The exemption does not specify the issuing government or institution, governing statute, geographic scope, or validity requirements. Operators could assert exemptions based on foreign or other licenses Congress did not intend to recognize.

20. **§ 3(b)—Grandfathering has no express limits on subsequent changes.** The bill does not address transfers, renewals, amendments, expanded areas, or increased production under a pre-enactment license. It also fails to state expressly that the exemption ends when the qualifying license expires, is revoked, or is suspended.

21. **§ 3(c)—The environmental-assessment exemption is unlimited.** Any activity conducted “for the purpose of environmental assessment” is exempt, with no quantity limit, necessity test, or restriction on sale of recovered minerals. Commercial operators could characterize substantial extraction as baseline research, impact assessment, or monitoring.

22. **§§ 3(b)–(c)—Exemptions lack verification and accountability procedures.** There is no advance approval, public disclosure, independent review, special reporting, or express authority to withdraw an exemption for abuse. The bill also does not allocate the burden of establishing eligibility, inviting disputes over how exemptions are proved.

### Registry and enforcement

23. **§ 4(a)—The registration obligation has no jurisdictional boundary.** “Each covered vessel” could be read to include foreign vessels operating entirely abroad with no U.S. connection. The bill should identify the relevant operators, flags, locations, or other jurisdictional links rather than leave that reach to litigation.

24. **§§ 4(a)–(b)—Registration and reporting mechanics are missing.** “Operator” is undefined, and there are no registration deadlines, update requirements, reporting due dates, required fields, or record-retention rules. Multiple owners, managers, and contractors could dispute who is responsible and when compliance is due.

25. **§ 4(b)—Self-certified reports provide weak detection safeguards.** The bill requires no independent verification, vessel tracking, inspection, sampling, or disclosure of quantities, coordinates, and exemption claims. Operators could omit information essential to establishing a violation while claiming to have described their “recovery activities.”

26. **§§ 4–5—Registry and reporting violations have no express penalties.** Section 5 penalizes only violations of § 3, not failure to register or report under § 4. Other laws may punish some false submissions, but this bill supplies no tailored sanction for noncompliance or incomplete reporting.

27. **§§ 3–5—No agency is expressly assigned enforcement responsibility.** NOAA administers the registry, but the bill does not designate who investigates mining violations, assesses penalties, or brings enforcement proceedings. It also lacks express implementing-rule authority, leaving important operational questions to existing authorities or litigation.

28. **§§ 4–5—Investigative and adjudicative procedures are missing.** The bill supplies no express inspection, subpoena, records-access, or evidence-preservation powers, and no procedure for assessing or contesting civil penalties. Existing agency or judicial powers may fill some gaps, but their availability and scope should not be assumed.

29. **§ 5—There is no tailored mechanism to stop ongoing mining or repair damage.** The bill does not expressly authorize cessation orders, injunctions, vessel detention, forfeiture, restoration, or recovery of cleanup costs. Monetary penalties alone may not promptly halt extraction, and other sources of such authority need to be checked.

30. **§ 5(a)—The daily violation unit is uncertain.** The text does not say whether separate vessels, sites, or operations generate separate penalties, or whether a violation continues on days without recovery. Combined with the annual production threshold, this creates uncertainty about which days are punishable and how penalties accumulate.

31. **§ 5(a)—The penalty may become a cost of doing business.** The provision sets a maximum but no express economic-benefit recovery, per-ton assessment, or repeat-offender enhancement. Depending on production value and enforcement practice, retaining mining proceeds could make violations financially attractive.

32. **§ 5(b)—“Willfully” leaves a consequential criminal-proof question.** The bill does not clarify what defendants must know about their conduct, illegality, production totals, or a Secretary’s risk determination. That ambiguity could make prosecutions harder, especially where the underlying prohibition is itself uncertain.

### International agreement, duration, and commencement

33. **§ 6—The international mandate does not require a binding prohibition.** “Seek to negotiate” imposes an effort obligation, not an obligation to secure an agreement, and the 18-month deadline does not clearly specify whether negotiations must begin or conclude. “International agreement” also does not require legally binding obligations, entry into force, compliance mechanisms, or domestic implementation.

34. **§ 6—The international agreement would replicate domestic loopholes.** Requiring prohibitions “equivalent to those in section 3” could carry forward the exploration and assessment exemptions and the narrow underlying mining definition. It does not clearly require a comprehensive global prohibition applicable to all relevant actors.

35. **§ 7(a)—The early-termination standard and procedure are underspecified.** “Without serious harm” does not identify ecological criteria, acceptable uncertainty, cumulative impacts, or whether all mining methods and environments must satisfy the finding. The bill also specifies no process for commissioning the National Academies report or ensuring its independence, publication, and scientific scope.

36. **§§ 7(a)–(b)—The automatic sunset defeats the scientific safeguard.** The entire Act expires after ten years even if Congress never finds mining safe and the National Academies identifies continuing serious risks. This creates a guaranteed pathway for mining to resume without meeting § 7(a).

37. **§ 7(b)—Sunset treatment of enforcement and records is unclear.** Expiration ends the registry and other provisions without an express savings clause for pending proceedings, accrued liabilities, investigations, or record retention. General federal savings law may preserve penalties already incurred, but the bill should expressly address the full transition.

38. **§§ 5(a), 8—The penalty commencement dates conflict.** Civil penalties purport to cover violations from enactment, but the Act—and thus the prohibition—does not take effect for 180 days. Attempts to penalize conduct in that interval would invite statutory and fair-notice challenges; the provisions should be harmonized.

39. **§ 8—The six-month delay permits continued and new operations.** Until the effective date, this bill does not prohibit mining or require registration. If an immediate halt is intended, the prohibition should take effect at enactment, with any administrative transition addressed separately.

40. **§§ 3, 7–8—Interaction with existing mining authorities is unresolved.** The bill does not expressly amend conflicting authorization provisions, identify the treatment of existing exploration licenses and commercial-recovery permits, or explain what happens to them when the prohibition ends. Although a later prohibition can supersede earlier permissions, express conforming amendments would reduce disputes over continued rights and agency obligations.
